name: master french onion vegetable soup
instructions:
TWO VARIANTS ON A SPECTRUM. This is a master recipe — variant A and variant B sit at two ends of an additive spectrum. Start from A (Julia Child's classical); add any subset of B's built-up ingredients to move toward B. Everything B adds stacks cleanly with A's base.

- VARIANT A — STANDARD JULIA CHILD FRENCH ONION SOUP: deeply caramelized onions + broth + white wine deglaze + toasted bread + broiled gruyere gratin. Nothing else in the pot.
- VARIANT B — CELEBRATORY / BUILT-UP: everything added — white beans, turmeric + fresh ginger, WHOLE mushrooms, TURNIPS (preferred) or celery root, and TARRAGON (new herb; see notes on why it fits here better than in any other french stew).

=== SHARED — CARAMELIZATION + WINE + BROTH + GRATIN ===

The whole recipe rests on the same 45-60 min deep-caramelization of yellow onions + white wine deglaze + broth simmer + toasted-bread + gruyere gratin finish. See DEEP CARAMELIZATION note.

FAT: butter + olive oil can be BALANCED, or lean toward olive oil (see FAT NOTE — butter isn't as flavor-load-bearing here as it is in something like the chicken/dumpling stew).

BROTH: dark vegetable bouillon (Better Than Bouillon) is best; standard vegetable stock also works; beef stock is the classical fallback.

BROTHY, NOT THICKENED: less flour than most stews. Ideally no flour at all — the finished soup should be brothy, not roux-thickened. If you want body, get it from the caramelized onions and (in variant B) the vegetables cooked down, not from flour.

=== VARIANT A — STANDARD JULIA CHILD ===

INGREDIENTS:
- 4-5 large yellow onions, thinly sliced
- 2-4 tbsp butter + 2-4 tbsp olive oil (balance to taste; can lean olive oil)
- 1 bay leaf
- fresh thyme (a few sprigs)
- 1/2 to 3/4 cup dry white wine
- 6-8 cups broth (dark vegetable bouillon preferred; standard vegetable stock or beef stock also work)
- 1 baguette, sliced into rounds and toasted
- shredded gruyere (generous)
- fresh parsley (finish)
- salt and black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. DEEPLY CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: butter + olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium-low heat. Add onions + pinch of salt. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, 45-60 min until deeply mahogany-brown. Don't rush.
2. DEGLAZE WITH WHITE WINE: pour in wine, scrape up fond, reduce briefly.
3. ADD BROTH + HERBS: pour in broth. Add bay leaf and thyme. Bring to simmer.
4. SIMMER: 10-15 min to integrate. Fish out bay leaf and thyme stems.
5. TASTE AND ADJUST: salt and pepper.
6. TOAST THE BREAD: rounds toasted crisp all the way through.
7. GRATIN + SERVE: ladle into oven-safe bowls. Top each with toast round(s) + generous gruyere. Broil until deeply melted and browned in spots (2-4 min; watch closely).
8. Fresh parsley on top. Serve immediately.

=== VARIANT B — CELEBRATORY / BUILT-UP ===

Everything variant A has, plus these additions (all stack additively — you can add any subset of them and land anywhere on the spectrum between A and B):

BUILT-UP ADDITIONS:
- WHITE BEANS (cannellini, great northern, or ideally corona/gigantes — see notes on large beans) — the only appropriate starch in this recipe (see NO POTATOES note).
- TURMERIC + FRESH GINGER — spice/herb axis addition (moves beyond A's thyme-only base).
- WHOLE MUSHROOMS — kept whole (not sliced) for visible-component texture. Portabella, shittake, or oyster all work.
- TURNIPS (PREFERRED) OR CELERY ROOT — coarse-chopped root vegetable component. Turnips outperform celery root here; see notes.
- CARROTS — coarse-chopped, alongside the turnips.
- GARLIC — a few cloves minced, added briefly before the wine deglaze.
- TARRAGON — new herb, fits this dish better than any other french stew I've cooked. See notes.

PROCEDURE (additive to variant A's flow):
1. Deep-caramelize onions same as variant A.
2. Add GARLIC briefly (~1 min) before deglazing.
3. Deglaze with white wine.
4. Add broth + bay leaf + thyme + TURMERIC + TARRAGON.
5. Add COARSE-CHOPPED TURNIPS (or celery root) + CARROTS + WHOLE MUSHROOMS + FRESH GINGER. Simmer 25-35 min until vegetables are tender.
6. Fold in WHITE BEANS. Simmer 10-15 min to integrate.
7. Taste and adjust; fish out bay leaf.
8. Toast the bread, gratin + serve as variant A. Fresh parsley on top.
notes:
=== DEEP CARAMELIZATION IS THE WHOLE TECHNIQUE ===

The onions need to go past standard softened-golden into deep-mahogany-brown territory. 45-60 min on medium-low, stirred occasionally — not high-heat-quick-sauté. The Maillard reaction across that long slow cook is what generates the sweet-savory-deep flavor that carries the whole soup. Under-caramelize and the soup reads thin and one-note-oniony.

You'll know it's right when the onions are visibly darker than golden — brown enough that you might worry you overcooked them — and the pot bottom has a substantial fond built up. That fond is what gets deglazed by the wine and dissolves into the finished broth.

=== A + B ARE A SPECTRUM — PURELY ADDITIVE ===

This isn't a hard fork between two dishes. Every ingredient variant B adds stacks cleanly on top of variant A's base — you can add any subset and land anywhere between them.

- Feeling low-effort? Do variant A. It's Julia Child's classical dish, and it's already excellent.
- Feeling celebratory? Do variant B — all the additions at once.
- Somewhere in between? Pick one or two of B's additions (e.g., just white beans; or beans + turnips + tarragon; or the full ginger/turmeric axis without the vegetables). Every subset works.

The spectrum is the point — this is a soup family with a clean base and a lot of legitimate extensions.

=== FAT — BUTTER + OLIVE OIL CAN BE BALANCED OR LEAN OLIVE OIL ===

Traditional french onion soup leans heavily on butter, but here the fat balance can go anywhere from butter-forward (like french-chicken-soup, where butter is a load-bearing flavor) to olive-oil-forward. The onion caramelization is the flavor carrier — butter isn't doing as much flavor work here as it does in a chicken/dumpling stew or a bechamel-based dish. Feel free to lean olive oil if you want a lighter finish, or 50/50 for balance, or butter-heavy if that's what you have. All work.

=== BROTH — DARK VEGETABLE BOUILLON PREFERRED (BETTER THAN BOUILLON); BEEF STOCK IS FALLBACK ===

DARK VEGETABLE BOUILLON (specifically Better Than Bouillon's dark vegetable base) works BETTER than beef base here. The deeply-caramelized onions carry the savory-hearty register on their own, and the dark vegetable bouillon extends that register more cleanly than beef base does. This is the OPPOSITE of french-beef-and-mushroom-stew, where beef stock wins.

Standard vegetable stock works fine but not as well as the concentrated dark bouillon.

=== BROTHY, NOT THICKENED — LESS FLOUR THAN OTHER STEWS ===

This dish should be brothy at the finish, not roux-thickened. Most french stews (french-beef-and-mushroom-stew variant B, coq au vin, etc.) use flour as a structural thickener. This one doesn't. If you want body, it comes from the caramelized onions and (in variant B) the vegetables cooked down — not from flour. Skip flour entirely, or use only a tiny pinch if you really want to.

=== TURNIPS OUTPERFORM CELERY ROOT HERE — UNUSUAL EXCEPTION ===

TURNIPS BEAT CELERY ROOT in this recipe. Reasons: turnips add real flavor to the broth (they don't just sit there as a texture component), and their earthy taste after being boiled fits this brothy dish's register better than celery root's cleaner, milder taste.

This is an UNUSUAL EXCEPTION for me — I normally declare celery root the winner over turnips (and over radishes) across most of my cooking. But here, boiled-turnip flavor + earthiness lands correctly against the caramelized onion + white wine + herb base in a way celery root doesn't. Celery root still works if that's what you have; turnips are the upgrade.

=== TARRAGON — FITS HERE BETTER THAN ANY OTHER FRENCH STEW ===

Tarragon is a NEW ingredient for this recipe and fits here better than in any other french stew I've cooked. Two comparisons:

- vs FRENCH CHICKEN STEW VARIANTS (french-chicken-soup, chicken-with-vinegar): in those, tarragon is either optional or gets outclassed by piney herbs (thyme, rosemary in some variants) that pair more assertively with chicken. Tarragon works there but isn't the standout.
- vs FRENCH-BEEF-AND-MUSHROOM-STEW: a comparable dark-broth stew but going in a different direction — red wine + tomato + rosemary axis. Tarragon may CLASH with red wine + tomato specifically (its anise-adjacent character doesn't extend the tomato register the way rosemary + bay do). Untested there but suspected clash.

Here in the french onion vegetable soup register (white wine + vegetable broth + no tomato + caramelized onions + optional root vegetables), tarragon lands cleanly and adds real dimension. Recommended for variant B.

=== WHITE BEANS FOLDED IN FOR PROTEIN ===

A can of white beans folded in during the simmer gives the soup a protein component that classical french onion soup lacks. The soup is traditionally about the onion + broth + cheese contrast, with no protein — this addition shifts the dish toward a fuller meal rather than a starter or side. In this master recipe, beans are the ONLY appropriate starch (see NO POTATOES note).

GOOD OPPORTUNITY FOR 'LARGE' WHITE BEANS (CORONA / GIGANTES): the generous broth + gratin format gives large beans room to be a distinct component on the spoon. Corona / gigantes are the upgrade when you can find them; cannellini or great northern are still totally fine.

=== NO POTATOES — CLASHING (BEANS ARE THE ONLY APPROPRIATE STARCH) ===

Potatoes are CLASHING in this recipe. They don't work here — potatoes are designed to pair with (pseudo)meat in a broth-based dish, not with the vegetable + bean set that defines this soup family. In this master, WHITE BEANS are the ONLY appropriate starch. The toasted-bread + gruyere gratin covers the crunchy-carb slot; the beans cover the soft-starch slot. Potatoes would push the dish toward a bland root-vegetable soup and duplicate the starch role that beans + gratin already handle.

Where potatoes DO belong: variant B of french-beef-and-mushroom-stew (with pseudo-meat), where they're explicitly load-bearing.

=== CHEESE — ALL 'GOOD CHEESE' WORKS HERE, BUT THE FUNKIER THE BETTER ===

Any good melting cheese works on top of this soup, but the FUNKIER the pick, the better the result. Ranked roughly:
- GOUDA and GRUYERE (top tier): funky, nutty, alpine-ish character melts cleanly and browns well under the broiler. Both are ideal.
- COMTÉ: close alternative to gruyere if you have it (also funky-nutty-alpine).
- PARMESAN and MONTERREY JACK: still work but less good — cleaner, less funky, don't carry the same depth against the caramelized-onion base.
- SHARP CHEDDAR: pushes the soup anglo and fights the french identity; avoid.

Use PLENTY regardless of pick — the gratin cheese layer should be substantial. Cheese covers the toast and drapes over the bowl's rim; that's the target visual.

=== TOAST THE BREAD FIRST ===

Untoasted bread on top of the soup goes soggy under the broiler and dissolves into the broth. Pre-toasted rounds hold their crisp structure even after floating in hot broth under melted cheese. Toast until crisp all the way through, not just surface-browned.

=== OVEN-SAFE BOWLS FOR THE BROILER STEP ===

Traditional presentation: individual oven-safe crocks/bowls that go directly under the broiler. If you don't have oven-safe bowls, broil the cheese on the toast separately on a sheet pan and float the finished cheese-toasts on top at serving.

=== TURMERIC ROLE — SECRET PINCH IN A, REAL HERB AXIS IN B ===

Turmeric plays two different roles across the variants:
- VARIANT A (if you want to add it): a small pinch as a SECRET INGREDIENT — makes the finished soup taste smokey without giving away where the flavor came from. Not classical; don't tell anyone.
- VARIANT B: a real herb/spice-axis ingredient (1/2 to 1 tsp) alongside fresh ginger. Structural component, not secret pinch.

=== WHY THE WHITE WINE + NO TOMATO + GINGER/TURMERIC IDEAS SUIT THIS DISH BUT NOT FRENCH BEEF STEW ===

An earlier attempt drafted a variant B set (celery root/turnips instead of meat + ginger/turmeric instead of rosemary/thyme + no tomato + white wine) as a pure-vegetable variant of french-beef-and-mushroom-stew. That variant was rejected there — the beef-stew register (red wine + tomato + rosemary) fought the additions rather than extending them.

The reason it works here: this soup is already built around white wine + no tomato + deeply-caramelized onions. Extending outward into celery root / turnips / carrots / ginger root / turmeric / tarragon keeps the register consistent.

=== WANT TO TRY — PARSNIPS IN VARIANT B ===

Parsnips are a candidate for variant B alongside the turnip/celery root register. Would fit the sweet-root-vegetable slot. Untested; log when tried.

=== PARSLEY AT THE FINISH ===

Chopped fresh parsley scattered on top of the finished bowl before serving.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- french-beef-and-mushroom-stew: comparable dark-broth stew that goes in a different direction (red wine + tomato + rosemary + meat). Different register on almost every axis; the WHY-WHITE-WINE-SUITS-THIS-DISH note above explains why the two families don't cross-fertilize easily.
- french-chicken-soup: french soup with chicken thighs + white wine + herbs + dumplings. Broth-forward format, different protein logic (chicken meat), same french-provincial axis. Butter plays a bigger flavor role there than here (see FAT note).
- lentil-mushroom-potato-stew: french/italian vegetable stew. Different structural logic (chunky stew vs onion-and-broth soup).
- coq-au-vin: french chicken braise with red wine and mushrooms. Different food; different wine axis (red vs white here).
